finding.claim: DELETE /files/<fid> deletes any file for any caller because the authorization result is discarded.
finding.source: Any HTTP DELETE to /files/<fid>; g.user is None when the header is absent.

trace.note: require_allowed (acl.is_allowed) called as a bare statement; return value ignored
is_allowed returns a bool and never aborts

finding.guards_checked: load_user (views.py:10-12) only sets g.user; no decorator; is_allowed returns False for None user but the result is unused; no abort. Fix: use ensure_allowed at views.py:18, as rename_file does at views.py:26.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. views.py:10-12 (load_user) only sets g.user from a request header and does not block. No auth decorator is on delete_file (views.py:15-16). views.py:18 calls require_allowed, which is the alias for acl.is_allowed (views.py:4), as a bare statement, so its bool result is discarded. acl.py:4 returns a bool and never aborts; acl.py:8-10 ensure_allowed, which does abort(403), is never called on this path. For a missing or None user, is_allowed returns False (acl.py:5), but nothing acts on that value, so views.py:19 runs regardless.
verdict.reason: The DELETE handler at views.py:18 discards the bool from require_allowed (alias of acl.is_allowed, acl.py:4-5) and then unconditionally runs `del STORE[fid]` at views.py:19, so any caller, including one with no X-Session-User-Verified header, can delete any stored file.

finding.claim: User identity is taken from a client-settable header, so an attacker can impersonate any user with grants, if the app is reachable without a proxy that strips and sets this header.
finding.sink: g.user used for authorization at views.py:18 and views.py:26, and in acl.py:5 grants.get(user).

trace.note: g.user set directly from request header with no verification

finding.guards_checked: None in this code. Safety depends on an upstream proxy that strips and rewrites the header, which cannot be verified from these files. Authentication change: flag for Security review (#ask-internal-security) before fixing. Fix: derive user from a server-verified session or token.

verdict.guard_found: None in the code. views.py:10-12 (load_user) copies the X-Session-User-Verified header into g.user with no check. The only possible guard is an upstream proxy that strips and sets the header, which is not in these files. acl.py:9-10 (ensure_allowed) is a real abort(403) guard, but it trusts the spoofable g.user. views.py:18 calls require_allowed (acl.is_allowed, a bool-returning function) as a bare statement, so its result is discarded and it is not an effective guard.
verdict.reason: The rename path is spoofable from the code alone (views.py:12 sets g.user from the header, views.py:26 and acl.py:5 trust it), but whether an attacker can reach the app with that header intact depends on a deployment proxy the code does not show, so reachability cannot be decided here. The trace is also misdescribed at views.py:18: require_allowed's bool result is discarded, so the DELETE handler performs no authorization at all, which is a separate, code-verifiable defect the candidate did not state.

finding.claim: Rename stores an unvalidated client-supplied name; a missing key causes a 500 and any JSON type or size is accepted.

trace.note: request.json['name'] read with no type or length validation; KeyError on missing key

finding.guards_checked: Authorization via ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) is correct. No input validation exists. Fix: require a non-empty string with a length limit, else return 400.

verdict.guard_found: ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) raises abort(403) when is_allowed (acl.py:4-5) returns False, and views.py:26 calls it as a bare statement that aborts on failure, so only users with a "write" grant reach views.py:27. No input validation exists on views.py:27.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (views.py:27 reads request.json["name"] with no validation, and acl.py:8-10 aborts with 403 for non-grantees), but the only party who can reach the unvalidated write is a user already granted "write" at views.py:26, who can already set the name, so the flaw gives no added power and is a robustness/input-validation bug rather than a security vulnerability.

finding.claim: Lookups use STORE[fid] before any authorization, and a missing ID returns 500 while an existing one returns 403 or 200, which reveals which IDs exist.
finding.source: The <fid> path segment in DELETE /files/<fid> and POST /files/<fid>/rename.
finding.sink: Response code differences from STORE[fid] lookup at views.py:17 and views.py:25.

trace.note: STORE[fid] raises KeyError for an unknown ID, which Flask turns into 500
Existing but unauthorized IDs receive 403, so the two responses differ

finding.guards_checked: No 404 handling and no uniform error response. Fix: use STORE.get(fid) and return 404 when missing; consider 404 for unauthorized access too.

verdict.guard_found: None effective against the existence oracle. views.py:17 and views.py:25 do an unguarded STORE[fid] lookup with no 404 handling, and nothing catches the KeyError. The only check on the rename path, ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10, called at views.py:26), returns 403 for existing IDs and is the source of the difference, not a control against it. On the DELETE path, require_allowed (acl.py:4, aliased is_allowed) is called as a bare statement at views.py:18 with its bool discarded, so it blocks nothing.
verdict.reason: Missing IDs raise KeyError at views.py:17 and views.py:25 and return 500, while existing IDs on rename return 403 via acl.py:10 and views.py:26, so the existence oracle is real for POST /files/<fid>/rename; the trace is misdescribed for DELETE, where views.py:18 discards is_allowed's result, so an existing ID returns 200 and is deleted for any user (a more severe authorization bypass the candidate missed).
